verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia and South Carolina both require only $25,000 per person in bodily injury liability coverage
verifiedClaims.note: Georgia: § 40-9-37(a) requires limits 'not less than the amounts specified in subparagraph (a)(1)(A) of Code Section 33-7-11', which reads '$25,000.00 because of bodily injury to or death of one person in any one accident, and, subject to such limit for one person, $50,000.00 ... two or more persons ... and $25,000.00 because of injury to or destruction of property'. South Carolina: § 38-77-140(A) 'twenty-five thousand dollars because of bodily injury to one person ... fifty thousand dollars ... two or more persons ... twenty-five thousand dollars because of injury to or destruction of property'. Also verified in sibling packs 1749, 1757, 4729, 4738.

verifiedClaims.claim: Bodily Injury Per Person | $25,000 | $25,000 — Bodily Injury Per Accident | $50,000 | $50,000 — Property Damage Per Accident | $25,000 | $25,000
verifiedClaims.note: First comparison table, three rows. Verified verbatim in both statutes. Optional: cite § 40-9-37 / § 33-7-11(a)(1)(A) and § 38-77-140 in the table caption.

verifiedClaims.claim: UM/UIM Required? | Offered; rejection must be in writing
verifiedClaims.note: First-table Georgia cell. § 33-7-11(a)(1): no auto liability policy may be issued 'unless it contains an endorsement or provisions undertaking to pay the insured damages ... sustained from the owner or operator of an uninsured motor vehicle'; (a)(3): 'The coverage required under paragraph (1) of this subsection shall not be applicable where any insured named in the policy shall reject the coverage in writing.' Precise wording: 'Included unless rejected in writing' is closer than 'offered' — the coverage is in the policy by default.

verifiedClaims.claim: UM/UIM Required? | Mandatory unless rejected in writing
verifiedClaims.currentValue: UM: mandatory on every policy at no less than the § 38-77-140 limits and cannot be rejected (S.C. Code § 38-77-150(A)). UIM (and UM above the minimum): optional — the insurer must offer it up to the liability limits on the Department-approved form (§ 38-77-160; § 38-77-350).
verifiedClaims.note: First-table South Carolina cell. § 38-77-150(A): 'No automobile insurance policy or contract may be issued or delivered unless it contains a provision ... herein referred to as the uninsured motorist provision ... within limits which may be no less than the requirements of Section 38-77-140.' There is no rejection mechanism for basic UM. § 38-77-160: carriers 'shall offer, at the option of the insured, uninsured motorist coverage up to the limits of the insured's liability coverage in addition to the mandatory coverage prescribed by Section 38-77-150' and 'shall also offer, at the option of the insured, underinsured motorist coverage'. The post collapses mandatory UM and optional UIM into one 'UM/UIM' that can be rejected; only the optional layers are accepted or rejected, and that happens on the § 38-77-350 form. Suggested cell: 'UM mandatory, cannot be rejected (§ 38-77-150); UIM optional but must be offered (§ 38-77-160)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: These minimums — often written as 25/50/25 — were set decades ago and have not kept pace with modern medical costs.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina's 25/50/25 minimums took effect for policies issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2007 (2006 Act No. 395). Georgia's took effect in the late 2000s (the § 33-7-11 history line was not read this run). Say 'set more than 15 years ago', not 'decades ago'.
verifiedClaims.note: History line under § 38-77-140: '2006 Act No. 395, SECTION 3.A, eff June 14, 2006 affecting policies issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2007.' Justia's annotations to § 33-7-11 reference the older Georgia $10,000/$15,000 minimums, confirming the 25/50/25 figure is a later amendment; its exact effective date was not verified. 'Decades ago' is not supportable for either state; 'more than 15 years ago' is safe for both.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11, Georgia insurers must offer UM/UIM coverage equal to the liability limits on every auto policy they issue. The policyholder can reject the coverage or select lower limits, but the rejection must be in writing.
verifiedClaims.note: Statute: UM limits 'at the option of the insured shall be: (A) Not less than $25,000.00 ... or (B) Equal to the limits of liability ... if those limits of liability exceed the limits of liability set forth in subparagraph (A) ... In any event, the insured may affirmatively choose uninsured motorist limits in an amount less than the limits of liability.' Rejection of the coverage itself must be 'in writing' ((a)(3)). Accurate as written; 'affirmatively choose' is the statute's phrase for selecting lower limits.

verifiedClaims.claim: If the insurer cannot produce a signed rejection form, the UM/UIM coverage defaults to the full liability limits of the policy.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Without a written rejection the UM coverage applies (§ 33-7-11(a)(3)); the amount is set by the insured's election under (a)(1) — the 25/50/25 minimum or limits equal to the liability limits — and the insured 'may affirmatively choose' less. The statute does not say a missing rejection form makes the coverage 'default to the full liability limits'.
verifiedClaims.note: The sentence overstates the statute. Suggested: 'If the insurer cannot produce a written rejection, UM/UIM coverage is part of the policy (O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11(a)(3)); how much depends on the limits the policyholder elected, up to the policy's liability limits.' Also add the election that actually decides claim value: 'added-on' coverage is the default and pays on top of the at-fault driver's limits; the insured may 'reject the coverage referenced in subdivision (I) ... and select in writing' reduced-by coverage, which pays only the difference (§ 33-7-11(b)(1)(D)(ii)(I)-(II)) — same finding as sibling pack 4709.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia also allows stacking of UM/UIM coverage across multiple vehicles on the same policy unless the policyholder has specifically waived stacking in writing. If you insure three vehicles and carry $100,000 in UM/UIM coverage per vehicle, you could potentially access $300,000 in underinsured motorist benefits.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia permits stacking across separate policies ('An insured has long been allowed to stack his multiple policies of uninsured motorist coverage' — State Farm v. Hancock, 164 Ga. App. 32 (1982); Dairyland Ins. Co. v. State Farm (Ga. App. 2008)), but not within one policy: 'as a general rule, there can be no stacking or pyramiding of the uninsured motorists provisions as to single policy coverage of automobiles' (Crafter v. State Farm, 251 Ga. App. 642 (2001)). There is no 'waiver of stacking in writing' in Georgia law; the written election that exists is added-on vs reduced-by under § 33-7-11(b)(1)(D)(ii).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Crafter v. State Farm Ins. Co., 251 Ga. App. 642, 554 S.E.2d 571 (2001); State Farm v. Hancock, 164 Ga. App. 32 (1982)
verifiedClaims.note: The claim is backwards on the one point that matters (same-policy stacking) and invents a written waiver. Hancock: https://law.justia.com/cases/georgia/court-of-appeals/2008/a07a1919-0.html is Dairyland (sibling 4709); Hancock at https://law.justia.com/cases/georgia/court-of-appeals/1982/64456.html. Rewrite the hypothetical: 'If you are an insured under three separate policies that each carry $100,000 in UM/UIM coverage, Georgia lets you stack them — potentially $300,000 (Hancock; Crafter). Coverage on several cars under a single policy generally cannot be stacked.'

verifiedClaims.claim: Under S.C. Code § 38-77-150, UM/UIM coverage is mandatory in South Carolina — it must be included in every auto policy unless the named insured rejects it in writing on a specific form approved by the Department of Insurance.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: UM at the § 38-77-140 minimums is mandatory in every policy and cannot be rejected (§ 38-77-150(A)). UIM, and UM above the minimum, are optional coverages the insurer must offer up to the liability limits (§ 38-77-160) on the form the Department of Insurance approves under § 38-77-350; the insured accepts or rejects them on that form.
verifiedClaims.note: § 38-77-350(A): 'The director or his designee shall approve a form that automobile insurers shall use in offering optional coverages required to be offered pursuant to law'; (B): a completed, signed form creates a conclusive presumption of 'an informed, knowing selection of coverage'. The post attaches the form and the rejection to § 38-77-150 (mandatory UM, no rejection); they belong to §§ 38-77-160/-350 (optional UIM/excess UM). Same finding as sibling packs 1757, 4729, 4738.

verifiedClaims.claim: Courts in South Carolina strictly interpret rejection forms, and an improperly executed rejection is void, meaning full coverage applies.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The rule is the 'meaningful offer' doctrine: the insurer bears the burden of proving it made a meaningful offer of UIM (commercially reasonable notice; limits specified; nature of the coverage explained; premium disclosed), and 'if the insurer fails to comply with its statutory duty to make a meaningful offer to the insured, the policy will be reformed, by operation of law, to include UIM coverage up to the limits of liability insurance carried by the insured' (State Farm v. Wannamaker, 291 S.C. 518 (1987); Progressive v. Leachman (S.C. 2005)). By statute, if the insured does not return the executed offer form within 30 days, 'the insurer shall add on uninsured motorist and underinsured motorist coverages with the same policy limits as the insured's liability limits' (§ 38-77-350(E)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Wannamaker, 291 S.C. 518, 354 S.E.2d 555 (1987); S.C. Code § 38-77-350(E)
verifiedClaims.note: The post's substance (a defective offer/rejection yields coverage at the liability limits) is right; the mechanism and vocabulary are not ('void rejection' vs. reformation for want of a meaningful offer), and it applies to optional UIM, not to mandatory UM. Leachman: https://law.justia.com/cases/south-carolina/supreme-court/2005/25919.html.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina also permits stacking of UM/UIM benefits under S.C. Code § 38-77-160. Stacking across multiple vehicles on the same policy, or even across policies in the same household, can significantly increase available coverage.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 38-77-160 limits stacking rather than granting it: an insured with UM/UIM above the basic limits 'is protected only to the extent of the coverage he has on the vehicle involved in the accident', and if none of the insured's vehicles was involved, 'only to the extent of coverage on any one of the vehicles with the excess or underinsured coverage'. Case law confines stacking to Class I insureds (named insured, spouse, resident relatives) and caps it at the coverage on the vehicle involved (Carter v. Standard Fire Ins. Co., 406 S.C. 609 (2013)).
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 38-77-160; Carter v. Standard Fire Insurance Co., 406 S.C. 609, 753 S.E.2d 515 (2013)
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from sibling packs 4729 / 1757 / 4738 and re-read in § 38-77-160 today. Suggested: 'South Carolina lets a named insured or resident relative (a Class I insured) stack UM/UIM from other household vehicles and policies, but only up to the coverage on the vehicle involved (§ 38-77-160; Carter, 2013).' Drop 'broadly interpreted by courts' in the comparison table — the courts have narrowed it.

verifiedClaims.claim: the at-fault driver often carries bare-minimum coverage
verifiedClaims.note: Characterization with no figure; 'often' is the hedge. Keep.

verifiedClaims.claim: Georgia: Modified Joint and Several Liability — Georgia applies a modified form of joint and several liability under O.C.G.A. § 51-12-33.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia has several liability only. § 51-12-33(b): the trier of fact 'shall ... apportion its award of damages among the person or persons who are liable according to the percentage of fault of each person. Damages apportioned by the trier of fact as provided in this Code section shall be the liability of each person against whom they are awarded, shall not be a joint liability among the persons liable, and shall not be subject to any right of contribution.'
verifiedClaims.note: Heading and lead sentence. 'Modified joint and several' is the wrong label; the statute abolishes joint liability for apportioned damages. Retitle 'Georgia: Several Liability Only — Each Defendant Pays Its Share'. The body's own next sentences ('Georgia generally applies several liability') and the table cell ('Generally several liability only') are right and can stay; drop 'generally'.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under Georgia's comparative fault system, a plaintiff can recover only if the plaintiff is less than 50% at fault.
verifiedClaims.note: § 51-12-33(g): 'the plaintiff shall not be entitled to receive any damages if the plaintiff is 50 percent or more responsible for the injury or damages claimed.' Matches the writer-profile table and sibling packs 1709/1722/1756. Also (a): damages reduced in proportion to the plaintiff's percentage of fault.

verifiedClaims.claim: However, if a defendant is found to have acted with specific intent to cause harm, that defendant may be held jointly liable for the entire judgment.
verifiedClaims.note: § 51-12-33 contains no intentional-tort or 'specific intent' exception to several liability; subsections (a)-(g) were read in full. The sentence appears to import another state's rule (e.g., Florida's § 768.81(4)). Delete it.

verifiedClaims.claim: As a practical matter, identifying multiple at-fault parties in Georgia is critical because each defendant's share of fault is capped at their percentage of responsibility. If two drivers share fault for a wreck that caused your traumatic brain injury, you pursue separate claims against each driver's policy.
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate consequence of (b). Worth one added clause: fault is also assessed against nonparties ((c), (d)), so an unnamed, uninsured wrongdoer's share is simply unrecoverable in Georgia — the strongest reason the section gives to find and name every defendant.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina maintains traditional joint and several liability for defendants found liable in a personal injury action. ... Any defendant found liable can be held responsible for the entire judgment, regardless of that defendant's individual percentage of fault. This is a significant advantage for plaintiffs, because it means you can collect the full judgment amount from whichever defendant has the deepest pockets or the largest insurance policy.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: South Carolina's joint and several liability is modified by S.C. Code § 15-38-15 (version effective January 1, 2026): 'joint and several liability does not apply to any defendant whose conduct is determined to be less than fifty percent of the total fault for the indivisible damages as compared with the total of: (i) the fault of all the defendants and tortfeasors; and (ii) the fault (comparative negligence), if any, of plaintiff. A defendant whose conduct is determined to be less than fifty percent of the total fault shall only be liable for that percentage' (§ 15-38-15(A)). A defendant at 50% or more remains jointly and severally liable, and under (F) a defendant 'whose conduct is determined to be wilful, wanton, reckless, or intentional or conduct involving the illegal or illicit use, sale, or possession of drugs ... shall be jointly and severally liable for all damages' regardless of percentage. Under (G) fault may be allocated to a nondefendant tortfeasor if disclosed within 180 days of commencement.
verifiedClaims.note: Most consequential legal error in the section: 'traditional' and 'regardless of that defendant's individual percentage of fault' are wrong, and have been since 2005. scstatehouse.gov publishes two versions ('Section effective until January 1, 2026' and 'Section effective January 1, 2026'); the 2026 version applies today and, unlike the prior text, its subsection (F) no longer lists alcohol-related or grossly negligent conduct — do not write 'a drunk driver is always jointly liable' without a separate read of the prior version and its transition rule. Rewrite: 'South Carolina keeps joint and several liability only for a defendant whose share is 50% or more of the total fault, or whose conduct was wilful, wanton, reckless, intentional or drug-related (S.C. Code § 15-38-15). A defendant below 50% pays only its percentage.' This is also the one place the post may cite § 15-38-15 — it governs apportionment among defendants, never the plaintiff's bar (profile rule).

verifiedClaims.claim: Under South Carolina's comparative fault rule, a plaintiff can recover if the plaintiff is less than 51% at fault.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Nelson v. Concrete Supply Co., 303 S.C. 243, 399 S.E.2d 783 (1991)
verifiedClaims.note: Reused from sibling packs 1709/1722/1756; matches the writer-profile table. If a citation is added it must be Nelson, never § 15-38-15.

verifiedClaims.claim: This difference matters enormously when one at-fault party has minimal coverage and another has a substantial policy. In South Carolina, you do not have to chase each defendant for their proportional share — you can collect the full amount from any one of them.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Only from a defendant whose share is 50% or more of the total fault, or whose conduct falls under § 15-38-15(F). A minor-share defendant pays only its percentage in both states.
verifiedClaims.note: Suggested: 'This difference matters when the deep-pocket defendant carries most of the fault: in South Carolina a defendant found 50% or more responsible can be made to pay the whole judgment, while in Georgia every defendant pays only its own share.'

verifiedClaims.claim: An umbrella policy typically provides $1 million to $5 million in additional coverage, and it activates once the underlying policy limits are exhausted.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: NAIC, Small Business Insurance (umbrella 'coverage limits typically range from $1 million to $5 million'); NAIC, A Shopping Tool for Homeowners Insurance (umbrella 'usually sold with policy limits of $1 million or more')
verifiedClaims.note: NAIC is the state-regulator association; the $1M–$5M range is its own figure for umbrella limits and the personal-lines guide gives '$1 million or more'. Keep, and attribute: '(NAIC)'. Also true by statute that umbrella/excess policies need not carry UM/UIM: S.C. Code § 38-77-161; O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11(a)(3) ('excludes umbrella or excess liability policies unless affirmatively provided for').

verifiedClaims.claim: The challenge is that umbrella policies do not appear on a standard insurance disclosure. In Georgia, you can discover additional coverage through formal discovery once a lawsuit is filed.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Georgia has a pre-suit disclosure statute that expressly reaches umbrella coverage: every liability insurer 'shall provide, within 60 days of receiving a written request from the claimant, a statement, under oath ... stating with regard to each known policy of insurance issued by it, including excess or umbrella insurance, the name of the insurer, the name of each insured, and the limits of coverage' (O.C.G.A. § 33-3-28(a)(1)); the insured must disclose the name of each known insurer within 30 days of a request ((a)(2)). The request is made under oath by certified mail or statutory overnight delivery.
verifiedClaims.note: The post has the two states reversed on this point: Georgia's statute is the broader one (any liability or casualty insurer, umbrella included, 60 days), while South Carolina's § 38-77-250 is limited to 'nonfleet private passenger' auto policies. Rewrite: 'In Georgia, a sworn written request under O.C.G.A. § 33-3-28 obliges every liability insurer — umbrella and excess carriers included — to disclose its policies and limits within 60 days, before any lawsuit is filed.'

verifiedClaims.claim: In South Carolina, S.C. Code § 38-77-50 requires insurers to disclose policy limits within 30 days of a written request by the claimant.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: The section is S.C. Code § 38-77-250, not § 38-77-50 (no § 38-77-50 exists in Chapter 77 as published on scstatehouse.gov). § 38-77-250(A): every automobile insurer that is or may be liable 'shall provide, within thirty days of receiving a written request from the claimant's attorney, a statement, under oath ... stating with regard to each known policy of nonfleet private passenger insurance issued by it, the name of the insurer, the name of each insured, and the limits of coverage'. The request must be under oath, sent by certified mail or statutory overnight delivery, state that the attorney is authorized to make it, and attach the incident report.
verifiedClaims.note: Three things wrong: the section number (cited three times — body, comparison table, 'Early coverage investigation'), the requester (the claimant's attorney, not the claimant), and the scope (nonfleet private passenger auto policies only — it does not compel disclosure of umbrella, excess or commercial policies, which is the opposite of what the umbrella section uses it for). Replace all three occurrences.

verifiedClaims.claim: the trucking company is required by federal law to carry at least $750,000 in liability coverage (and often carries $1 million or more)
verifiedClaims.currentValue: 49 CFR § 387.9, Table 1: for-hire carriers in interstate or foreign commerce with a GVWR of 10,001 lbs or more hauling nonhazardous property — $750,000; oil and most hazardous materials — $1,000,000; the listed high-hazard classes — $5,000,000.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified. Precision: the $750,000 floor applies to for-hire interstate carriers of nonhazardous property with a GVWR of 10,001 lbs or more, and rises to $1 million or $5 million for hazardous cargo — so 'often carries $1 million or more' is partly a legal requirement, not only a market habit. Optional cite inline: '(49 C.F.R. § 387.9)'.

verifiedClaims.claim: A solo driver might carry $25,000 in personal coverage
verifiedClaims.note: Hypothetical pegged to the statutory minimum; 'might' keeps it hypothetical.

verifiedClaims.claim: the employer may be directly liable under the doctrine of respondeat superior — Latin for "let the master answer." Both Georgia and South Carolina recognize this doctrine, which holds employers responsible for the negligent acts of employees committed within the scope of employment.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: S.C. Code § 15-38-15(C)(3)(a) (vicarious responsibility 'by reason of agency, employment, or other legal relationship'); Cornell LII Wex, respondeat superior
verifiedClaims.note: Black-letter doctrine in both states; § 15-38-15(C)(3)(a) itself directs that an employer 'vicariously responsible for the conduct of another defendant' be treated as a single party with that defendant, which confirms South Carolina's recognition in the very statute this post must cite. 'Directly liable' is slightly off — respondeat superior is vicarious liability; the direct theories are the negligent hiring/entrustment claims in the next paragraph. Suggested: 'vicariously liable'. (Sibling pack 1650 covers workers' compensation, not this doctrine.)

verifiedClaims.claim: Beyond respondeat superior, employers can face direct liability for negligent hiring, negligent training, negligent supervision, or negligent entrustment of a vehicle to an unqualified driver. These claims are independent of the employee's own liability and open up additional coverage pools.
verifiedClaims.note: General statement of recognized direct-negligence theories; no figure or citation asserted. Keep.

verifiedClaims.claim: Product liability claims against manufacturers and distributors typically involve corporate insurance policies worth tens of millions of dollars.
verifiedClaims.note: No source for the 'tens of millions' figure. Keep the sentence without the number: 'Product liability claims against manufacturers and distributors are paid from corporate policies that dwarf a personal auto policy.'

verifiedClaims.claim: In Georgia, the homestead exemption is $21,500 of equity.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: O.C.G.A. § 44-13-1: exempt from levy and sale 'any real or personal property or both of a debtor in the amount of $5,000.00 or $21,500.00 for real or personal property that is the debtor's primary residence'. In bankruptcy, § 44-13-100(a)(1): 'not to exceed $21,500.00 in value' in the residence, or $43,000 'in the event title to property used for the exemption ... is in one of two spouses who is a debtor'.
verifiedClaims.note: Verified on both sections (both amended to $21,500 effective May 2, 2012). The figure is right for a judgment creditor (§ 44-13-1) and in bankruptcy (§ 44-13-100). Add the citation and, optionally, the $43,000 married-debtor figure. § 44-13-100 URL: https://law.justia.com/codes/georgia/title-44/chapter-13/article-2/section-44-13-100/.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina's homestead exemption is $63,250 for individuals (with a separate exemption for heads of household).
verifiedClaims.currentValue: S.C. Code § 15-41-30(A)(1)(a): 'The debtor's aggregate interest, not to exceed fifty thousand dollars in value, in real property or personal property that the debtor or a dependent of the debtor uses as a residence', with 'the aggregate value of multiple homestead exemptions allowable with respect to a single living unit' capped at $100,000. Under (B) the dollar amounts are adjusted for Southeastern CPI every even-numbered year, effective July 1, with the adjusted figures published in the State Register by the Revenue and Fiscal Affairs Office. The adjusted amount in force since July 1, 2026 could not be retrieved this run (RFA's '2026 Bankruptcy Limitation' link, sc.gov/media/11479, and the 2024 link both return 404).
verifiedClaims.note: $63,250 is a stale inflation-adjusted figure from an earlier cycle and is superseded twice over (2024 and 2026 adjustments). 'Separate exemption for heads of household' is not in the statute — the second figure is the $100,000 cap on multiple owners of one residence. Because the current adjusted number is unverifiable, do not print one: 'South Carolina's exemption is $50,000 in the statute, indexed to inflation every two years (S.C. Code § 15-41-30), so the current figure is higher.' Also note § 15-41-30 applies to judgment collection and bankruptcy alike ('exempt from attachment, levy, and sale under any mesne or final process issued by a court or bankruptcy proceeding').

verifiedClaims.claim: These exemptions protect the defendant's primary residence up to the stated amount, but any equity above the exemption is fair game.
verifiedClaims.note: True as to the exemptions, but the section omits the bigger limit on 'personal assets': a negligence judgment is dischargeable in bankruptcy. Add: 'A judgment for ordinary negligence can be wiped out in bankruptcy; the exceptions that matter here are a judgment for death or personal injury caused by the defendant's operation of a motor vehicle while intoxicated (11 U.S.C. § 523(a)(9)) and one for willful and malicious injury (§ 523(a)(6)).' § 523(a)(9) text verified: 'for death or personal injury caused by the debtor's operation of a motor vehicle, vessel, or aircraft if such operation was unlawful because the debtor was intoxicated from using alcohol, a drug, or another substance'. Wage garnishment is also capped: Georgia at the lesser of 25% of disposable earnings or the amount above $217.50 a week (O.C.G.A. § 18-4-5(a)(2)), which the writer may cite if the section discusses wages.

verifiedClaims.claim: When an insurance company unreasonably refuses to settle a claim within policy limits, it may be liable for bad faith — and bad faith damages can far exceed the original policy limits. This is one of the most powerful tools for recovering beyond policy limits, but the rules differ significantly between Georgia and South Carolina.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Southern General Ins. Co. v. Holt, 262 Ga. 267, 416 S.E.2d 274 (1992); Tyger River Pine Co. v. Maryland Casualty Co., 170 S.C. 286, 170 S.E. 346 (1933)
verifiedClaims.note: Accurate as a description of the failure-to-settle tort in both states, provided the section says whose claim it is: it belongs to the insured (the at-fault driver), and the injured person reaches it by assignment — exactly what happened in Holt ('Holt assigned her claim against Southern General for negligent or bad faith refusal to settle within the policy limits to Fortson'). Add one sentence to that effect at the top of Option 6.

verifiedClaims.claim: Under O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, if an insurer refuses to pay a covered claim within 60 days of a demand and the refusal is in bad faith, the insurer is liable for a penalty of up to 50% of the claim amount plus reasonable attorney's fees. Georgia courts have interpreted this statute to apply when an insurer unreasonably delays or denies a claim without a good faith basis for doing so.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 33-4-6 is a first-party statute: the demand must be 'made by the holder of the policy' and the penalty runs to 'such holder' — 'not more than 50 percent of the liability of the insurer for the loss or $5,000.00, whichever is greater, and all reasonable attorney's fees'. It gives an injured third party no claim against the at-fault driver's insurer (Mills v. Allstate, 288 Ga. App. 257 (2007): § 33-4-6 is 'in favor of the insurer's policy holder', and the third-party provision, § 33-4-7, 'applies only to an insurer's bad faith in responding to claims for property damage'). For a claim on the reader's own uninsured/underinsured-motorist coverage the operative penalty is § 33-7-11(j): if the UM insurer refuses to pay 'within 60 days after a demand has been made by the insured' and the refusal is found to be in bad faith, it owes 'not more than 25 percent of the recovery or $25,000.00, whichever is greater, and all reasonable attorney's fees', determined in a separate action after judgment.
verifiedClaims.note: Same misapplication corrected in sibling packs 1709, 1722 and 1744, and here it is worse because the section is titled 'Bad Faith Claims Against the Insurer' inside a post about the at-fault driver's policy. Rewrite the paragraph around the reader's own carrier: 'Georgia's statutory bad-faith penalty, O.C.G.A. § 33-4-6, protects policyholders against their own insurer ... it does not apply to a demand on the other driver's liability carrier. When the claim is on your own UM/UIM coverage, the penalty is the one in O.C.G.A. § 33-7-11(j): up to 25 percent of the recovery or $25,000, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees, after a 60-day demand.' § 33-4-6 text at https://law.justia.com/codes/georgia/title-33/chapter-4/section-33-4-6/ (sibling-verified); § 33-7-11(j) read today.

verifiedClaims.claim: Additionally, Georgia recognizes a common-law bad faith cause of action against the at-fault driver's own insurer. When a liability insurer fails to settle within policy limits despite having a clear opportunity to do so, and the insured is subsequently hit with an excess judgment, the insurer may be liable for the full amount of the judgment — even the portion exceeding policy limits. This creates enormous leverage in negotiations.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Southern General v. Holt (Ga. 1992): 'An insurance company may be liable for damages to its insured for failing to settle the claim of an injured person where the insurer is guilty of negligence, fraud, or bad faith in failing to compromise the claim'; 'In deciding whether to settle a claim within the policy limits, the insurance company must give equal consideration to the interests of the insured'; but 'An insurance company does not act in bad faith solely because it fails to accept a settlement offer within the deadline set by the injured person's attorney.' The claim is the insured's; in Holt the insured assigned it to the injured claimant, and Cotton States v. Brightman (Ga. 2003) restates the rule as liability 'for the excess judgment entered against its insured'.
verifiedClaims.sourceName: Southern General Ins. Co. v. Holt, 262 Ga. 267, 416 S.E.2d 274 (1992); Cotton States Mut. Ins. Co. v. Brightman, 276 Ga. 683 (2003)

Brightman: https://law.justia.com/cases/georgia/supreme-court/2003/s02g1739-1.html.

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina addresses insurer bad faith under S.C. Code § 38-59-20, which prohibits unfair claim settlement practices.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: § 38-59-20 lists 'improper claim practices' (misrepresenting coverage, failing to acknowledge communications promptly, failing to investigate, 'not attempting in good faith to effect prompt, fair, and equitable settlement of claims, including third-party liability claims ... in which liability has become reasonably clear', etc.) when done 'without just cause and performed with such frequency as to indicate a general business practice'. It is enforced by the Department of Insurance; it creates no private damages claim, and South Carolina 'does not recognize a third party action for the bad faith refusal to pay insurance benefits' (Kleckley v. Northwestern Nat'l Cas. Co., 338 S.C. 131 (2000)).

verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina also recognizes a common-law cause of action for bad faith refusal to pay benefits. Under South Carolina law, an insured can recover actual damages, consequential damages, and punitive damages when an insurer acts in bad faith.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Nichols v. State Farm (S.C. 1983): tort action for bad-faith refusal to pay first-party benefits; consequential damages not limited by the contract; punitive damages where the insurer's conduct was wilful or in reckless disregard of the insured's rights. Statutory companion: § 38-59-40 — attorney's fees (capped at one-third of the judgment) when an insurer refuses to pay the policyholder's claim for 90 days after demand 'without reasonable cause or in bad faith'.

Make the audience explicit: this is the reader's remedy against the reader's own UM/UIM carrier, not against the other driver's insurer (Kleckley). Add § 38-59-40 (sibling-verified). verifiedClaims.claim: South Carolina courts have held that a liability insurer has a duty to act in good faith when evaluating settlement offers within policy limits. If the insurer unreasonably rejects a within-limits settlement demand and the insured faces an excess verdict, the insurer can be held responsible for the full judgment amount. Punitive damages in South Carolina bad faith cases can be substantial, depending on the egregiousness of the insurer's conduct.
verifiedClaims.currentValue: Tyger River Pine Co. v. Maryland Casualty Co. (S.C. 1933): insurer that refused to settle within the $5,000 limit was liable to its insured for the $7,000 verdict; codified by reference in § 38-59-40(3) ('Nothing in this section may be construed to alter or affect the Tyger River ... doctrine'). Restated in Doe v. S.C. Med. Malpractice Liab. JUA, 347 S.C. 642 (2001): 'An insurer who unreasonably refuses or fails to settle a covered claim within the policy limits is liable to the insured for the entire amount of the judgment obtained against the insured regardless of the limits contained in the policy.'
